title: How would you design a recommendation system — start simple (trending/popular, recent activity, category-based rules) before ML, then collaborative filtering (users who liked X also liked Y) vs content-based filtering (similar item attributes), offline precomputation of recommendations vs real-time ranking, event tracking for feedback, and the cold-start problem for new users/items?
shortTitle: How would you design a recommendation system
topicTitle: How would you design a recommendation system

s1_definition.profdef: A recommendation system suggests relevant items to a user by combining simple heuristics and machine-learning models. You start with non-ML baselines (trending, popular, recent activity, category rules) that are cheap and surprisingly effective, then add collaborative filtering (recommend what similar users liked) and content-based filtering (recommend items with attributes similar to what the user liked). Heavy candidate generation is precomputed offline in batch, while a lightweight ranking layer orders candidates in real time using fresh context. A feedback loop tracks user events (views, clicks, purchases) to continuously retrain, and the cold-start problem, having no history for new users or items, is handled with popularity, content attributes, and onboarding signals.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh logs into National Bank of India's app, it suggests products: "Customers like you took a home loan", "Based on your fixed deposit, consider a recurring deposit". The simplest version just shows the most popular products this month (trending), which already helps. A smarter version notices that customers similar to Rajesh, same age, same savings pattern, often took a home loan, so it suggests that (collaborative filtering). Another angle notices Rajesh already holds a fixed deposit, so it suggests similar savings products (content-based). The bank prepares most of these suggestions overnight in bulk (offline precompute) and only does a quick final re-ordering when Rajesh actually opens the app (real-time ranking), learning from what he taps (feedback).
s1_definition.oneliner: Start with popularity and rules, add collaborative and content-based filtering, precompute candidates offline and rank in real time, close the loop with event feedback, and handle cold-start with popularity and attributes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A recommendation system suggests relevant items to a user by combining simple heuristics and machine-learning models. You start with non-ML baselines (trending, popular, recent activity, category rules) that are cheap and surprisingly effective, then add collaborative filtering (recommend what similar users liked) and content-based filtering (recommend items with attributes similar to what the user liked). Heavy candidate generation is precomputed offline in batch, while a lightweight ranking layer orders candidates in real time using fresh context. A feedback loop tracks user events (views, clicks, purchases) to continuously retrain, and the cold-start problem, having no history for new users or items, is handled with popularity, content attributes, and onboarding signals.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh logs into National Bank of India's app, it suggests products: "Customers like you took a home loan", "Based on your fixed deposit, consider a recurring deposit". The simplest version just shows the most popular products this month (trending), which already helps. A smarter version notices that customers similar to Rajesh, same age, same savings pattern, often took a home loan, so it suggests that (collaborative filtering). Another angle notices Rajesh already holds a fixed deposit, so it suggests similar savings products (content-based). The bank prepares most of these suggestions overnight in bulk (offline precompute) and only does a quick final re-ordering when Rajesh actually opens the app (real-time ranking), learning from what he taps (feedback).

**One line to remember:** Start with popularity and rules, add collaborative and content-based filtering, precompute candidates offline and rank in real time, close the loop with event feedback, and handle cold-start with popularity and attributes.

sections.s2_technical:
Start simple before ML. The biggest mistake is jumping to a deep-learning model on day one. Simple baselines deliver most of the value cheaply: trending items (most engaged with recently), all-time popular items, recent activity (continue where you left off), and category rules (if a customer has a savings account, suggest a fixed deposit). These need no training, are easy to reason about, give an immediate baseline to beat, and serve as the fallback when smarter methods have no signal. You only add ML when the simple methods plateau.

Collaborative filtering. This recommends based on behavior patterns across users: "users who liked X also liked Y". It needs no knowledge of item attributes, only the user-item interaction matrix (who engaged with what). User-based collaborative filtering finds users similar to you and recommends what they liked; item-based finds items frequently engaged with together. At scale you factorize the huge sparse interaction matrix into latent vectors (matrix factorization) so each user and item is a small vector, and a recommendation is a dot product. Its strength is discovering non-obvious connections; its weakness is cold-start, because a brand new user or item has no interactions.

Content-based filtering. This recommends items whose attributes are similar to items the user already liked. You represent each item as a feature vector (category, risk level, tenure, interest rate) and recommend items close to the user's profile of liked items. Its strength is that it works for new items (a new product has attributes even with zero interactions) and gives explainable recommendations ("because you hold a fixed deposit"). Its weakness is that it stays within what the user already likes and does not surface surprising cross-category items the way collaborative filtering can. In practice you blend both into a hybrid, which is what most real systems do.

Offline precomputation versus real-time ranking. Generating candidates, scoring every item for every user, is expensive and cannot run on the request path for millions of users and items. So you split into two stages. Offline, in nightly or hourly batch, you precompute a candidate set per user (say the top few hundred relevant items) and store it. Online, when the user opens the app, a lightweight ranking layer takes those precomputed candidates and re-orders them using fresh real-time context (time of day, what they just viewed, current session) and applies business rules and filters. This two-stage candidate-generation-then-ranking design is how large systems hit low latency while still using heavy models.

Event tracking and the feedback loop. Recommendations improve only if you learn from outcomes. You instrument the app to emit events: impressions (what was shown), clicks, conversions (opened a product), and dwell time. These events stream into a data pipeline and become training labels, so the model learns which recommendations actually worked. You also measure online with A/B tests, comparing click-through and conversion of a new model against the current one before rolling it out. Without this loop, you are guessing.

The cold-start problem. New users and new items have no interaction history, so collaborative filtering cannot help them. You handle it in layers. For a new user, show popular and trending items and use any onboarding signals (what they selected at signup, their demographics) and fall back to content-based once they have a liked item or two. For a new item, use its content attributes to place it near similar items and give it some exploratory exposure so it can gather interactions. Over time, as history accumulates, collaborative filtering takes over. This graceful degradation from popularity to content-based to collaborative is the heart of handling cold-start.

The senior nuance is that a recommendation system is a pipeline of fallbacks and a blend, not one algorithm. You layer popularity, content-based, and collaborative, pick the best available signal for each user, precompute the expensive part, rank cheaply in real time, and continuously retrain from feedback. You also guard against feedback loops that trap users in a filter bubble by injecting some exploration (occasionally showing diverse items), and you respect compliance, because in banking you cannot recommend products a customer is not eligible for.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India recommends financial products to customers. Rajesh (SAV2001) holds a savings account and a fixed deposit; Priya (CUR3001) holds a current account. A brand new customer has no history.

Problem 1 — the app recommended the same generic banner to everyone. It ignored what each customer already held and what similar customers did. This is why we add collaborative and content-based filtering to personalize.

Problem 2 — scoring every product for every customer live was too slow. This is why we precompute candidate recommendations offline and only rank them in real time when the customer opens the app.

Problem 3 — new customers got no useful suggestions because collaborative filtering had no history for them. This is the cold-start problem, handled by falling back to popular and trending products and onboarding signals.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo: a `PopularityRecommender` (baseline), a `CollaborativeRecommender` (users who hold X also hold Y), a `ContentBasedRecommender` (similar product attributes), a `HybridRecommender` that blends and handles cold-start, an offline `CandidateStore`, and a real-time `Ranker`. It recommends for Rajesh (rich history), Priya (some history), and a new customer (cold-start), and records feedback events.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a catalog, holdings (Rajesh holds a fixed deposit, Priya holds a credit card, two other customers hold various products), popularity counts, and a new customer with no holdings.

Step 1 (offline precompute): For Rajesh, who holds a fixed deposit, the hybrid recommender runs. Collaborative filtering sees that other customers who hold a fixed deposit also hold a home loan and a recurring deposit, so those score. Content-based sees Rajesh holds a savings-category product and suggests the recurring deposit (same category). Popularity nudges everything. The blended top candidates are stored for Rajesh.

Step 2 (offline precompute): For Priya, who holds a credit card, collaborative filtering finds fewer co-holders, so content and popularity carry more weight. Candidates are stored.

Step 3 (cold-start): The new customer has zero holdings, below the minimum interactions threshold, so the hybrid recommender skips collaborative filtering entirely and falls back to the most popular products. Those are stored as the new customer's candidates. This is graceful cold-start handling.

Step 4 (real-time): Rajesh opens the app in the evening. The ranker takes his precomputed candidates and re-orders them with fresh context (business rules, session), returning the final short list instantly, because the heavy work was done offline.

Step 5 (feedback): Rajesh taps the home loan recommendation. The event tracker records a CLICK on HOME_LOAN for SAV2001. This event becomes a training label so the model learns that recommending a home loan to a fixed-deposit holder worked.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] cold-start for NEWCUST → popularity + content fallback
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Rajesh (holds FD, rich signal): [HOME_LOAN, RECURRING_DEPOSIT, PERSONAL_LOAN]
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] FEEDBACK SAV2001 CLICK on HOME_LOAN → training signal
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Priya (holds credit card):      [FIXED_DEPOSIT, HOME_LOAN, CREDIT_CARD]
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] New customer (cold-start):       [FIXED_DEPOSIT, HOME_LOAN, CREDIT_CARD]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Offline (batch, nightly) ──
  Interaction matrix (holdings) + catalog + popularity
    │
    ▼
  HybridRecommender per user
    │ collaborative (0.5): co-holders of FD also hold HOME_LOAN
    │ content (0.3): FD is savings → suggest RECURRING_DEPOSIT
    │ popularity (0.2): global nudge
    │ cold-start? → popularity fallback
    ▼
  CandidateStore (top 200 per user, precomputed)

  ── Online (request, milliseconds) ──
  Rajesh opens app (evening)
    │
    ▼
  Ranker.rank(candidates, context)
    │ fresh session signals + eligibility filters + exploration 10%
    ▼
  Top 3: [HOME_LOAN, RECURRING_DEPOSIT, PERSONAL_LOAN]
    │
    ▼  Rajesh clicks HOME_LOAN
  EventTracker → feedback event → training pipeline → retrain model
       (closes the loop: next time recommendations are better)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I design a recommendation system as a layered pipeline of fallbacks and a blend, not a single algorithm, and I deliberately start simple before any machine learning. Simple baselines, trending items, all-time popular products, recent activity, and category rules like suggesting a fixed deposit to a savings customer, deliver most of the value cheaply, need no training, are easy to reason about, and give me a baseline to beat and a fallback when smarter methods have no signal. On my project at National Bank of India this alone beat the generic one-size-fits-all banner we started with. I only add ML once the simple methods plateau.

The two ML approaches I combine are collaborative filtering and content-based filtering. Collaborative filtering recommends based on behavior patterns across users, the classic users who liked X also liked Y, using only the interaction matrix of who engaged with what, and at scale I factorize that sparse matrix into small latent vectors so a recommendation becomes a dot product. Its strength is discovering non-obvious connections, like fixed-deposit holders tending to take home loans, and its weakness is cold-start because a new user or item has no interactions. Content-based filtering recommends items whose attributes are similar to what the user already liked, representing each product as a feature vector of category, risk, and tenure, which works for brand-new items and gives explainable recommendations like because you hold a fixed deposit, but tends to stay within what the user already likes. So I blend them into a hybrid, which is what real systems do.

For performance I split into offline precomputation and real-time ranking, because scoring every item for every user cannot run on the request path. Offline, in nightly or hourly batch, I generate a candidate set of a few hundred relevant items per user and store it. Online, when the customer opens the app, a lightweight ranker takes those candidates and re-orders them with fresh context like time of day and the current session, applies business rules and eligibility filters, and returns the final short list instantly. This two-stage candidate-generation-then-ranking design is how I get both heavy models and low latency.

Recommendations only improve with a feedback loop, so I instrument the app to emit impressions, clicks, conversions, and dwell time, stream those events into a pipeline where they become training labels, and A/B test a new model against the current one on click-through and conversion before rolling it out. The cold-start problem I handle with graceful degradation: a new user sees popular and trending items plus any onboarding signals, a new item is placed near similar items by its content attributes and given some exploratory exposure, and as history accumulates collaborative filtering takes over. I also inject a little exploration so users are not trapped in a filter bubble, and in banking I always respect eligibility and compliance so I never recommend a product the customer cannot take.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I start with popularity and rules, add collaborative and content-based filtering blended into a hybrid, precompute candidate sets offline and rank them cheaply in real time, close the loop by tracking events and A/B testing retrained models, and handle cold-start by gracefully degrading from collaborative to content-based to popularity so every user, new or established, gets useful recommendations.
